item.title: Tell HN: Scribd Breached
item.description:
Source: news.ycombinator.com

Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026:

Subject: Notice of Security Incident

This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.

Hello,

We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.

We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).

We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.

Watch for phishing

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.
For more information

We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.

The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.
We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.

Scribd, Inc.

Top Comment:

I'd feel a lot better if I knew some red team security researchers were going hard trying to break into critical national infrastructure, just to ensure it's not too easy, but probably this isn't happening because it would be a felony to even try. The bad guys are free to try though.

All this will tend to get blamed on AI, but AI didn't put these vulnerabilities into place. AI is just a tool that can be used to discover vulnerabilities, and the only question we have to answer is whether or not that tool should be available to regular people.

Some will try to frame the question as being about whether we should allow AI aid in cyber-security, but that's not the question. This technology isn't going away. The bad guys will have it. Nations will have it. Again, the question is, can regular people also continue to have it?

item.title: Digital minimalism
item.description:
Source: vitalik.eth.limo

Top Comment:

I'm a social media luddite stuck in the 90's.

I didn't tweet or frequent twitter even before Musk took over. I'm too long-winded for tweets. I grudgingly made a Facebook account back when there was pressure to do so, neglected it, and then forgot about it entirely. Ditto for Linkedin. I frequent and post only on message boards that permit anonymity because I subscribe to the 90's mindset that, if the message is sound, it shouldn't matter who writes it. There are subs on reddit that I used to post to that would let you submit your credentials for flair so people would know you knew what you were talking about. I never did that for the same reason. Then I stopped posting on Reddit because I didn't like the moderation or the management. I still read it sometimes, but less than I used to.

These days, I see posting on social media as screaming into a void that is increasingly just AI slop. It feels good to scream sometimes, but it is a waste of time and effort. If raising my standards for where I scream causes me to spend less time screaming, that's just fine. I've started writing personal journals, ideas, etc. that I publish nowhere. It's, honestly, more satisfying and it breaks you free from any influence from upvotes, downvotes, mods, etc.. Writing for an audience of just yourself is actually pretty awesome.

I've concluded that the people running most social media today really don't want people like me around. Every update just seems to make things worse. Reddit, for example, has become unusable for me without reddit enhancement suite and the ability to turn pretty much every recent interface update off. RES is being sort of maintained, for now. Is RES minimalist? Moreso than firefly. It's also not its own app, which is great. I really don't want apps for everything. Give me a browser plugin so I can use a website like a website. When RES goes, Reddit will be dead to me.

Kudos to the folks here, at Hacker News, for not giving in to enshittifying urges.

item.description:

Top Comment:

Some notes I've got about this:

- MPTCP is not a requirement, it is a generic use-after-free.

- Exploitability over the internet is unlikely, most ISP routers drop packets with IP options fields.

- At least according to Red Hat, dropping packets with IP options yourself helps, but is not a full mitigation.

- Successful exploit requires multiple CPU cores to process packets, so systems with just a single core or packet processing pinned to a single core are not affected.

item.title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
item.description:
Source: thedataexchange.media

Top Comment:

I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the generator provably generates the correct mass scale assertions.

This is how formal methods can constrain AI for large systems.

We're doing this at the Open Markets Initiative, where we've generated millions of lines of Lean 4, TLA+, and Rocq that ensure that our open source electronic trading protocol code is accurate. We didn't expect it but the Lean prover did identify some incorrect steps. https://github.com/Open-Markets-Initiative
